title: nth term of linear sequences
examples: How do I find the rule for this sequence?
If the common difference is negative, how does that affect the nth term?
Can you show me how to check if a number belongs to a sequence?

explain.say: Today we learn about finding the rule for linear sequences. A linear sequence just means the difference between terms is always the same. This constant value is called the common difference.

To find the common difference you just subtract any term from the term that comes right after it. For example, look at the sequence two, five, eight. You subtract two from five, which gives you three. So the common difference is three.

The nth term formula helps us find any number in the sequence without listing them all out. The general form is n times the common difference plus the starting value minus the difference. For our example, the rule is three n plus one.
Now we check if a number is in the sequence. We take the number and plug it into the nth term formula and see if we get a whole number for n. If n is a positive whole number, then yes, it is a term.

items: Check if n is positive whole number

faq.a: The common difference is the constant amount added or subtracted each time to get from one term to the next. You can find it by subtracting any term from the next one. You might also ask what the constant gap is, or what the difference between terms is.
asks: What is the gap between terms?
How do I find the constant difference?

faq.q: How do I find the nth term?
faq.a: You can use the formula n times the common difference plus the first term minus the common difference. For example, if the sequence starts at four with a difference of two, the rule is two n plus two. You might also ask for the general formula, or how to write the rule.
asks: What is the formula for the nth term?
How do I write the rule for this sequence?

faq.q: Can I test if 100 is a term?
faq.a: Yes, you substitute 100 into the nth term formula and solve for n. If the value you get for n is a positive whole number, then 100 is definitely a term in the sequence. You might also ask if the number belongs, or if 100 is in the sequence.

faq.q: Does the common difference have to be positive?
faq.a: No, the common difference can be negative, which means the sequence is counting down. For instance, three, two, one has a common difference of negative one. You might also ask if the difference can be negative, or what happens if it decreases.
asks: What if the numbers get smaller?

faq.q: Does the nth term formula work for the first term?
faq.a: Yes, it must work for the first term. If you substitute n equals one into the formula, you should get the very first number in the sequence. You might also ask if n=1 gives the correct answer, or to check the first term.
asks: If n equals one, what do I get?
Does the formula match the first number?

facts: A linear sequence has a constant difference between consecutive terms.
The common difference is found by subtracting any term from the following term.
The nth term formula allows you to find any term without listing all previous terms.
If solving for n gives a whole number, the number belongs to the sequence.

quiz.say: The sequence is 5, 11, 17, 23. What is the common difference?
quiz.why: You subtract 5 from 11, which equals six. This is the constant difference.

wrong.0: This is the second term itself, not the difference.
wrong.1: This is the sum of the first two terms, which is incorrect.
wrong.2: This is the last term shown, not the difference.

quiz.say: Find the nth term for the sequence 3, 7, 11, 15.
quiz.why: The common difference is four. The rule is four n plus the starting value minus the difference, which is four n plus three minus four, giving four n minus one.

wrong.1: This incorrectly uses the first term as the constant part.
wrong.2: This subtracts the common difference twice.
wrong.3: This uses the wrong common difference of three.

quiz.say: Is 103 a term in the sequence 3, 7, 11, 15...? (Use the formula 4n - 1)
quiz.show: Is 103 a term? Solve for n.
quiz.why: When you solve 4n minus 1 equals 103, you get 4n equals 104, so n equals 26. Since 26 is a whole number, 103 is a term.

wrong.0: You might think the formula does not fit the number.
wrong.2: You might assume it is not a term because it is a large number.
wrong.3: This results from dividing 102 by 4, which is incorrect algebra.
